headline_en: Why are 39 percent of young people idle?
summary_en: A column by Ali Riaz reads recent Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics surveys together: 39.88% of youth aged 15-24 are not in education or work, employment is not growing, and many young people see leaving the country as the answer. It cites figures on how many job-seekers go abroad each year, on educated youth wanting to emigrate, and on Bangladeshi asylum applications in Europe, and blames growth-focused economic policy.

facts.statement: The Bangladesh Sample Vital Statistics 2023 survey report (Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics) says about 39.88% of youth aged 15 to 24 are neither in education nor in work, about 1 crore 22 lakh people; the rate was 40.66% in 2022. The same report puts Bangladesh's total population at 17 crore 15 lakh.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh Sample Vital Statistics 2023 (BBS), cited by columnist Ali Riaz

facts.statement: The BBS labour force survey published at the end of 2023 put the number of unemployed at 23.5 lakh at the end of the October-December quarter, 40 thousand more than a year earlier, an unemployment rate of 3.3%; the columnist says the definition of unemployment used is unrealistic.
facts.source_in_article: BBS labour force survey, cited by Ali Riaz

facts.statement: According to government statistics at least 20 lakh people enter the job market in Bangladesh each year; 13-14 lakh of them find work inside the country and the rest go abroad, so the number of unemployed has stayed between 24 and 28 lakh for two decades.
facts.source_in_article: Government statistics as cited by Ali Riaz

facts.statement: A 2023 survey by BRAC University and the Bangladesh Youth Leadership Center found 42% of the country's educated youth spoke of moving abroad (reported by Bonik Barta, 17 November 2023).
facts.source_in_article: BRAC University and BYLC survey via Bonik Barta, cited by Ali Riaz

facts.statement: The BBS 2022 labour force survey said that late in the year Bangladesh had about eight lakh educated (graduate) unemployed, 12% of the total. A recent BIDS study found 28% of students from colleges under the National University were still unemployed three years after passing (Prothom Alo, 24 March 2024).
facts.source_in_article: BBS 2022 labour force survey; BIDS study, cited by Ali Riaz

facts.statement: A Reuters report of 1 March (2024) said the number of Bangladeshis seeking asylum in Europe 'last year' was 40,332; the year before, 33,731 had applied (Prothom Alo, 1 March 2024).
facts.source_in_article: Reuters, cited via Prothom Alo by Ali Riaz

facts.statement: The columnist writes that some less-educated Bangladeshis go abroad for jobs legally and others go by illegal routes, and that migrants often die crossing the Mediterranean, with Bangladeshis a notable number among them.
About 41% of people aged 5 to 24 in Bangladesh are outside formal educational institutions, slightly lower than the previous year but far above 2019 (29%) and 2020 (28%) (Prothom Alo, 26 March 2024).
facts.source_in_article: BBS figures via Prothom Alo, cited by Ali Riaz

facts.statement: Income inequality in Bangladesh was 0.482 in 2016 and 0.499 in 2022; consumption inequality was 0.324 in 2016 and 0.334 in 2022. Government foreign borrowing has reached USD 100 billion.

key_quote_bn: সরকারি পরিসংখ্যান অনুযায়ীই বছরে কমপক্ষে ২০ লাখ মানুষ চাকরির বাজারে প্রবেশ করেন। তাঁদের মধ্যে ১৩-১৪ লাখের দেশের অভ্যন্তরে কর্মসংস্থান হয়। বাকিরা দেশের বাইরে প্রবাসে যান।

headline_en: Expatriate services will be taken to the grassroots: state minister for expatriates' welfare
summary_en: At the closing workshop of the first phase of Helvetas's SIMS project in Dhaka on 21 March 2024, State Minister Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury said technical training centres (TTCs) would be overhauled, new training equipment bought, Probashi Kallyan Bank branches increased and an expatriate welfare cell opened. The article also gives the project's coverage and results.

facts.statement: State Minister for Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Shafiqur Rahman Chowdhury said an initiative would be taken to overhaul the technical training centres (TTCs) and that new training equipment would be bought to make migrants skilled.

The state minister said Probashi Kallyan Bank branches would be increased across the country and a 'Probashi Kallyan Cell' (expatriate welfare cell) would be launched to deliver services at the grassroots level.

Member of Parliament Tanvir Shakil Joy said many problems remain with pre-departure training for aspiring migrants and that the gaps must be identified and fixed; making migrants skilled needs coordinated, not scattered, efforts.

Helvetas Swiss Intercooperation's SIMS project (first phase) was implemented in 23 upazilas of Cumilla, Narsingdi and Chattogram. It made about 10 lakh people aware of safe migration, trained about one lakh potential migrants on how to take a migration decision, and trained about 3,500 families in financial management and linked them to markets to start small businesses.

The closing meeting and lesson-learning workshop of the SIMS project's first phase was held at the Bangabandhu International Conference Centre, Dhaka; speakers included BMET Director General Saleh Ahmed Mozaffor and Swiss embassy representative Irene Hofstetter (আইরিন হফসটেটর), chaired by Helvetas Bangladesh Country Director Benjamin Blumenthal, with the keynote by project director Abul Basar and development consultant Hasan Imam Shaon.

headline_en: Turkey to take 200 workers, salary 51 thousand taka
summary_en: BOESL published a notice to recruit 100 male and 100 female garment/textile workers for Eurotex Textile company in Turkey at USD 470 a month. The article lists eligibility, contract terms, how to apply, the BDT 56,350 payable to BOESL and the 15 March 2024 deadline.

facts.statement: Bangladesh Overseas Employment and Services Limited (BOESL) published a recruitment notice for male and female garment workers for Eurotex Textile company of Turkey: 200 workers in total from Bangladesh, 100 men and 100 women.

Post 1 in the BOESL Turkey (Eurotex Textile) notice, printed as 'Texturising worker' (টেক্সটার্সিং ওয়ার্কার), 100 posts for men: at least SSC or equivalent, height at least 5 feet 3 inches, proficient in spoken English, experience in the relevant work, age 18 to 35.

Post 2 in the BOESL Turkey (Eurotex Textile) notice, 'Spinning, dyeing, garment worker', 100 posts for women: at least SSC or equivalent, height at least 5 feet 3 inches, proficient in spoken English, experience in spinning and dyeing work, age 18 to 35.
Salary for both posts at Eurotex Textile, Turkey, is USD 470 a month (about BDT 51,000).

Terms for the Eurotex Textile (Turkey) jobs via BOESL: two-year labour contract, renewable; three-month probation; eight hours' duty a day with overtime under Turkish labour law; accommodation borne by the company; food while at work borne by the company; airfare paid by the company; one day off a week; other benefits as per Turkish labour law.

Interested candidates had to apply through a BOESL link with a CV in English, educational qualifications, experience and other information; BOESL screens applicants and prepares a preliminary list, and a company representative interviews candidates for final selection.

Finally selected workers for Eurotex Textile, Turkey, must deposit a pay order of BDT 56,350 in total at BOESL covering BOESL's service charge and incidental expenses; the worker must also bear the Turkish embassy visa fee.
The application deadline for the BOESL Turkey (Eurotex Textile) recruitment was 15 March 2024.

key_quote_bn: চূড়ান্তভাবে নির্বাচিত কর্মীদের বোয়েসেলের সার্ভিস চার্জ এবং আনুষঙ্গিক ব্যয়সহ মোট ৫৬ হাজার ৩৫০ টাকার পে অর্ডার বোয়েসেলে জমা করতে হবে এবং তুরস্ক দূতাবাসের ভিসা ফি কর্মীকে বহন করতে হবে।

headline_en: CWCS consultation: no assurance of legal protection for women migrant workers
summary_en: At a consultation at Probashi Kallyan Bhaban on 7 March 2024, the Centre for Women and Children Studies (CWCS) presented a policy review saying women migrant workers lack assured legal protection abroad and face stigma and rejection on return. Officials spoke on service delivery, and the Probashi Kallyan Bank MD described eased loan terms for returnee women.

facts.statement: A CWCS policy review on returnee women workers says women migrant workers' situation is so risky that proper legal protection is not assured, they live under strict control, and they suffer physical abuse at various stages of the migration process.
facts.source_in_article: CWCS policy review presented by CWCS president Ishrat Sharmin

facts.statement: CWCS says women workers who return to Bangladesh are also at risk: most people view them negatively, assuming they came back after physical abuse, and in some cases husbands or families do not want to take them back.

The CWCS paper says women are forced to go abroad by discrimination and abuse such as child marriage, dowry pressure, husbands' multiple marriages and divorce; abroad, non-payment of wages, low wages and inability to save make it hard to meet the family's minimum needs.

Selim Reza, full-time member of the 'National Human Rights Council' (জাতীয় মানবাধিকার পরিষদ, as printed), said he saw the dire condition of Bangladeshi workers when he went to Saudi Arabia for hajj, asked where the accountability is of those who sent them, and said he has heard the same problems in the migration sector for 20 years with no progress.
facts.source_in_article: Selim Reza, full-time member, জাতীয় মানবাধিকার পরিষদ

facts.statement: Selim Reza referred to Bangladesh sending 'more than 13 lakh workers a year'.

Md. Khairul Alam, additional secretary of the expatriates' welfare ministry, said a worker coming for a service must not be made to run around; the country has enough laws to protect human rights but those implementing them and delivering services badly lack positive goodwill.

Probashi Kallyan Bank Managing Director Md. Mojibur Rahman said loan conditions for returnee women migrants have been much eased: they can get a loan even without a fixed address (when a husband or family does not accept them), there is no service charge on their loans, and no equity is needed for loans up to BDT 1 lakh; but few applications from women workers are received.
facts.source_in_article: Probashi Kallyan Bank MD Md. Mojibur Rahman

facts.statement: CWCS worked for four years (2020 to 2023) on a project to empower returnee women migrants in two upazilas of Dhaka, Keraniganj and Nawabganj, arranging various work for them through training.

headline_en: Deshi Dining restaurant in Qatar gives expatriate drivers a special discount card
summary_en: A Bangladeshi-owned restaurant in the Aziziya area of Qatar launched a discount card for Bangladeshi expatriate drivers, inaugurated on 26 February 2024 by Ambassador Md. Nazrul Islam. Card holders and up to three companions get 20% off any food.

facts.statement: Deshi Dining Restaurant, owned by young Bangladeshis and located in the Aziziya area of Qatar, launched a special discount card for expatriate Bangladeshi drivers; Bangladesh's ambassador to Qatar Md. Nazrul Islam inaugurated it on the night of Monday 26 February 2024 and handed cards to drivers.

With the Deshi Dining discount card in Qatar, Bangladeshi expatriate drivers get 20% off any food, and three more people accompanying a driver can buy food at the same discount; after using the card at least 15 times in a month, drivers get a card again for the next month.
facts.source_in_article: Restaurant; chief executive director Shakil Ahmed

facts.statement: Shakil Ahmed of Deshi Dining said Bangladeshi expatriate drivers in Qatar cannot cook for themselves because of their busy work.
facts.source_in_article: Shakil Ahmed, chief executive director of the restaurant

headline_en: More than BDT 200 crore in migration loans approved through MyGov in a year
summary_en: An a2i press release of 21 November 2026 says Probashi Kallyan Bank has approved over BDT 200 crore in migration loans applied for online through the government 'MyGov' platform since the service started on 3 December of the previous year. Over 10,000 outbound workers applied; approval now takes 3 to 4 days; the loan is up to BDT 3 lakh at 9% interest and is available at 122 branches.

facts.statement: Since the migration loan service for outbound workers was launched on the government digital platform 'MyGov' on 3 December 'last year' (2025), Probashi Kallyan Bank has approved more than BDT 200 crore in loans in about a year, and more than 10,000 outbound workers have applied online.
Through MyGov, the time from application to approval of a Probashi Kallyan Bank migration loan is now 3 to 4 days.

Under the MyGov migration loan service, an outbound worker can borrow up to a maximum of BDT 3 lakh at 9% interest from Probashi Kallyan Bank; the loan amount is set after verifying the worker's actual cost of going abroad.
facts.source_in_article: a2i programme press release (reported as 'it is learnt')

facts.statement: After an initial pilot, the digital (MyGov) migration loan service is now running at 122 branches of Probashi Kallyan Bank.

Previously applicants for a migration loan had to visit the bank branch several times to submit papers; with the online MyGov service they can apply from home and track the application's progress, reducing trips to the bank and reliance on middlemen, especially for workers from remote areas.

A survey published by Probashi Kallyan Bank found that the digital loan service cut applicants' time, travel and application-related cost by 50% each, cut the workload of the offices concerned by 30%, and cut paper use in the application process by 100%.

'MyGov' is the integrated government digital service platform run under the Cabinet Division and the ICT Division with a2i's technical support; citizens can apply for various government services, pay set fees, track applications and get digital certificates from home.

headline_en: Bangladeshis must not be allowed to become bait on any country's battlefield
summary_en: In parliament on Monday 9 November 2026, reserved-seat MP Rehana Akter said Bangladeshis lured to Russia with false job promises were handed to the Russian army and sent to the Russia-Ukraine war, with 54 deaths in three years and bodies not returned. She demanded joint action by three ministries, punishment of traffickers, compensation and repatriation. The rest of the article covers unrelated notices by other MPs (lake pollution, roads, factory stimulus, dengue, schools, hospitals).

facts.statement: MP Rehana Akter told parliament that a group of Bangladeshis went to Russia on the false lure of assured jobs and hope of a better life, taking high-interest loans and selling their homesteads; instead of the promised jobs they were handed over to the Russian army and, after training, deployed in the Russia-Ukraine war.
facts.source_in_article: Reserved-seat MP Rehana Akter, in parliament

facts.statement: Rehana Akter said 54 Bangladeshis have died in the past three years (in the Russia-Ukraine war) and many have been maimed; the bodies of those killed on the battlefield have still not been handed over to their families, who also face continuing pressure from lenders.
Citing media reports, MP Rehana Akter said human traffickers now trap people not only by posing as brokers but also by using modern technology such as AI deepfakes, social media and cryptocurrency.

Rehana Akter called on the expatriates' welfare, home and foreign ministries to take joint technological and diplomatic steps, and demanded punishment of traffickers, compensation for victims' families, and the quick return of Bangladeshis who are on the battlefield in Russia; she drew the expatriates' welfare minister's attention under rule 71.

named_actors.name: Rehana Akter

headline_en: Gunfight between joint forces and human traffickers in Teknaf, army soldier killed
summary_en: On the evening of Thursday 5 November 2026, a joint army-BGB-police team raided a deep hill area at Rangikhali, Teknaf, Cox's Bazar, where intelligence said an armed trafficking gang was holding about 120 Rohingya and Bengali people hostage. Army soldier Md. Titas Sheikh (27) was shot dead; 57 hostages were rescued and five gang members detained.

facts.statement: According to ISPR, intelligence indicated that an armed human-trafficking group of 15 to 16 people was holding about 120 Rohingya and Bengali people hostage in the deep hills of the Rangikhali area of Teknaf, Cox's Bazar.

A joint team of the Bangladesh Army's 10 Infantry Division, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and local police reached the Rangikhali hills, Teknaf, about 5 pm; traffickers opened fire and a gunfight followed. The joint forces rescued 57 hostages, detained five members of the trafficking gang and recovered a pistol, a locally made gun and four bullets.

Army soldier Md. Titas Sheikh (27), of Laskardia village, Nagarkanda upazila, Faridpur (father Afzal Hossain), was shot in the left shoulder in the gunfight with traffickers in Teknaf and was declared dead at the Combined Military Hospital, Ramu.
facts.source_in_article: ISPR; 16 APBn commander Additional DIG Md. Kawsar Sikder

headline_en: Expatriates protest in front of the Saudi embassy in Berlin
summary_en: Bangladeshi expatriates protested outside the Saudi embassy in Berlin on Friday 30 October 2026 over Saudi Arabia's execution of two Bangladeshi migrant workers, and handed in a signed protest letter demanding accountability, transparency and justice. Organisers criticised the Bangladesh authorities for saying they knew nothing until the media reported it.

facts.statement: Two Bangladeshi migrant workers were tried, sentenced to death and executed in Saudi Arabia; according to the protest organisers, the Bangladesh authorities said they knew nothing beforehand and learnt of it only after media reports.

Bangladeshi expatriates held a protest with posters in front of the Saudi Arabian embassy in Berlin at midday on Friday 30 October 2026 against the execution of two Bangladeshi expatriates in Saudi Arabia.

Concerned Bangladeshi citizens living in Berlin delivered to the Saudi embassy a protest letter addressed to the Saudi ambassador, with signatures of a large number of expatriates, demanding accountability, transparency and justice over the execution of two Bangladeshi migrant workers; the text attaches the date 14 October 2026 to this sentence without making clear whether it is the date of the execution or of the letter.

The organisers said the government's first reaction should have been to express concern or demand an explanation, and that they saw no formal reaction from Jamaat-e-Islami or NCP; they said ties with Saudi Arabia (diplomatic, economic, labour market) matter but kneeling on citizens' lives and dignity to protect them is unacceptable.

key_quote_bn: অথচ বাংলাদেশের কর্তৃপক্ষ বলছে, আগে কিছুই জানত না। সংবাদমাধ্যমে খবর প্রকাশের পর বিষয়টি তাদের নজরে এসেছে।

headline_en: Tightening of Australia's visa policy: what should Bangladeshi students and migrants do?
summary_en: An opinion piece by a teacher-researcher at Charles Darwin University argues that Australia's recent student-visa reforms, including the 'Genuine Student' requirement introduced in March 2024, aim to protect the system's integrity, and that students must respect visa purposes and conditions. It also calls on Australia for clear, timely decisions and on Bangladesh to negotiate bilaterally and act against unauthorised and fraudulent education and migration consultancies.

facts.statement: Australia introduced the 'Genuine Student' requirement in March 2024, after which some student visa application procedures changed further; the writer says the aim is to separate genuine intent to study from attempts to use a student visa mainly as a means of employment or long stay.
facts.source_in_article: Opinion writer (teacher and researcher, Charles Darwin University)

facts.statement: The writer says changing institution after arriving in Australia is not in itself unethical (financial difficulty, suitability of the course or personal circumstances can justify it), but enrolling at a reputed university only to obtain the visa with no intent to study there, then moving to a cheaper institution, damages the credibility of genuine students and responsible institutions.

The writer states that working within the permitted limit alongside study is understandable given Australia's high cost of living, but the student visa's main purpose is education, not to serve as an alternative work visa.

Some visa refusal or cancellation decisions in Australia can be legally reviewed; new visa applications, bridging visas and the right to seek review are subject to specific legal conditions, so the idea that using these processes lets a person stay in Australia indefinitely is wrong.

Advice in the article: international students must understand the educational purpose of their visa, temporary workers must follow their employment and visa conditions, and prospective migrants should decide on the basis of realistic qualifications and legal opportunities.

The writer warns that some dishonest intermediaries in Bangladesh mislead applicants with unrealistic guarantees of study, jobs or permanent residence abroad, or give incomplete or wrong information about visa conditions, real costs, academic eligibility or actual migration prospects in order to take money.

The writer urges the Bangladesh government to identify unauthorised operations, investigate fraud complaints, punish where needed and hold overseas education and migration consultancies accountable, and to provide reliable official information, a way to verify authorised service providers and awareness programmes for prospective students and migrants.

The writer says long delays in visa decisions create uncertainty for genuine students and skilled professionals who may then choose other countries, and that people who have already made major financial and academic commitments under existing rules should get reasonable transitional arrangements when policy changes.

The writer says attracting skilled workers and international students matters especially for regional Australia such as the Northern Territory, where institutions like Charles Darwin University contribute to building the local skilled workforce, so regional needs should be considered within the national visa system.

The writer proposes regular bilateral talks in which Bangladesh raises visa-policy changes, transparency of the application process, genuine students' problems and prospects for legal migration of skilled workers, with coordination among the Bangladesh High Commission, ministries, educational institutions and Australian authorities.

key_quote_bn: শিক্ষার্থী ভিসার প্রধান উদ্দেশ্য শিক্ষা গ্রহণের সুযোগ দেওয়া; বিকল্প কর্মসংস্থান ভিসা হিসেবে কাজ করা নয়।

headline_en: Legal notice seeks full disclosure on the two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia
summary_en: On Sunday 25 October 2026 Supreme Court lawyer Tasmiah Nuhiya Ahmed sent a legal notice to the foreign secretary, the expatriates' welfare secretary and the Wage Earners' Welfare Board director general seeking full information and preservation of records on the two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia, and on steps to protect other Bangladeshis detained abroad and at risk of execution. A preliminary reply was demanded within 24 hours, failing which a High Court writ would be filed.

facts.statement: Supreme Court lawyer Tasmiah Nuhiya Ahmed sent a legal notice by registered post to the foreign secretary, the expatriates' welfare and overseas employment secretary and the director general of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board, seeking disclosure of full information and preservation of documents on the two Bangladeshis executed in Saudi Arabia.
facts.source_in_article: Lawyer Tasmiah Nuhiya Ahmed, to Prothom Alo

facts.statement: The notice asks the authorities to state in writing when and how they learnt of the two persons' detention, trial, sentence and execution, what diplomatic steps were taken before and after, what information and documents have been obtained, why any information is still missing and whether there is a timetable to complete the work, and how records are being preserved.
The notice also asks what steps have been taken to protect Bangladeshi citizens detained abroad and at risk of the death penalty.

The notice demands a written preliminary reply and action within 24 hours of receipt; the lawyer said that on failure she would take legal steps including a writ petition in the High Court under Article 102 of the Constitution.
Related headlines embedded in the article say Bangladesh sent Saudi Arabia a letter seeking answers to six questions about the execution of the two.

named_actors.name: Tasmiah Nuhiya Ahmed

key_quote_bn: একই সঙ্গে বিদেশে আটক ও মৃত্যুদণ্ডের ঝুঁকিতে থাকা অন্য বাংলাদেশিদের সুরক্ষায় নেওয়া পদক্ষেপ সম্পর্কেও জানতে বলা হয়েছে নোটিশে।

headline_en: 20 more Bangladeshis on Saudi list of the 'convicted'; like Nazrul and Sweety, their sentences were not disclosed either
summary_en: A list of 2,461 Bangladeshi prisoners sent by the Saudi foreign ministry on 30 September 2026 marks 22 as 'convicted' with the 'summary of verdict' column blank; two of them, Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter, were later executed. On 19 October the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah wrote asking for the verdict summaries of the rest and, in a second letter, for release, pardon and remission for categories of prisoners. Saudi replies were not yet known.

facts.statement: On 30 September 2026 the Saudi foreign ministry sent a list of 2,461 Bangladeshi prisoners held in jails within the jurisdiction of the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah; some have court verdicts against them and others' cases are ongoing.
facts.source_in_article: Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah sources / documents seen by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: In the Saudi list, 22 Bangladeshi prisoners have 'convicted' in the 'status' column but the 'summary of verdict' column is blank, with neither type nor length of punishment; the Jeddah consulate does not know their sentences. The consulate's letter did not give the number; Prothom Alo counted 22 in the attached 9-page list.
facts.source_in_article: Prothom Alo's count of the attached list

facts.statement: Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter, whose executions in Saudi Arabia angered people in Bangladesh, were among the 22 listed as 'convicted' with no sentence stated; the fate of the other 20 is uncertain.

On 19 October 2026 the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah wrote to the Makkah region branch (Jeddah) of the Saudi foreign ministry asking it to coordinate with the authorities and quickly send the verdict summaries, saying the information is needed for consular duties, to update its database and to give citizens the best consular service.
facts.source_in_article: Consulate letter; Consul General Md. Shakhawat Hossain

facts.statement: Of the 22 Bangladeshis listed as convicted without sentence details in Saudi Arabia: 8 were tried for murder, 5 for drug trafficking, 5 in 'private rights' cases, 2 for violating state laws, 1 for cybercrime and 1 for adultery.
facts.source_in_article: Sources at the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah, from the Saudi list

facts.statement: Of the 22: six are in Dhahban (জাহবান) prison in Jeddah, six in Shumaisi, four in Jeddah General Prison, and the other six in Najran, Khamis, Al-Baha, Haddah and the Jeddah women's prison. All five 'private rights' prisoners are in Shumaisi.
facts.source_in_article: Sources at the Bangladesh consulate in Jeddah

facts.statement: The article explains that 'private rights' cases in Saudi Arabia are usually about personal claims or compensation, and that under Saudi law a murder case can end in qisas (death penalty) or be settled by blood money or imprisonment, so the type of case does not reveal the sentence.

Without a verdict summary the consulate cannot tell which options are open to a convicted Bangladeshi in Saudi Arabia: whether an appeal is possible, how a lawyer is to be appointed, or whether a blood-money settlement or pardon initiative can be pursued; all depend on the verdict.

In a second letter on 19 October 2026 the Jeddah consulate divided the 2,461 prisoners into five categories and requested: quick release and return home of those whose terms have ended, inclusion of well-behaved prisoners in the royal pardon list, remission of remaining sentences for first-time and minor-offence detainees, and quick disposal of pending cases.
The Jeddah consulate also wrote to the Saudi ministry about two more Bangladeshis whose families said security forces had arrested them without the families knowing why or from where.
As of 22 October 2026 the Saudi authorities' reply to the Jeddah consulate's letters was not known.

A second Bangladeshi, Md. Nasrullah Badarpuri, was also killed and 24 Bangladeshis were reported injured at the time.

facts.statement: On 10 October 2026 a missile attack by the Iran-backed Houthi armed group on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 14 people including Bangladeshi worker Md. Shahed Ahmmad.
facts.source_in_article: Expatriates' welfare ministry press release, 22 October 2026

facts.statement: Shahed's body was scheduled to land at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at 8:35 am on Friday 23 October 2026 and to be received at cargo gate no. 8 by State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam.

Shahed, of Madla village, Shajahanpur upazila, Bogura (father Md. Rafiqul Islam, mother Shahera Begum), worked as a plumber on a Jeddah project under a Saudi contracting firm and held a valid work permit (iqama). He had come home on leave because of his brother's death and was killed at the airport while returning to his workplace in Jeddah via Riyadh.

A second Bangladeshi, Md. Nasrullah Badarpuri of Badarpur village, Nangalkot upazila, Cumilla, was also killed in the Riyadh airport attack; the foreign and expatriates' welfare ministries said at the time that 24 more Bangladeshis were injured.

summary_en: On Sunday 18 October 2026 foreign ministry secretary (bilateral) Md. Nazrul Islam met Saudi ambassador Abdullah bin Zafar H bin Abiyah in Dhaka and handed over a diplomatic note asking about the execution of two Bangladeshis in Makkah and why Bangladesh was not informed beforehand. The same note had gone from the Jeddah consulate to the Saudi foreign ministry on 15 October; the ambassador said he would get details from Riyadh.

facts.statement: On Wednesday (about 14 October 2026) media in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere in the Middle East reported that two Bangladeshis, a woman and a man, had been executed in Makkah on charges of 'immoral acts' in a mosque area; the article says the executions took place 'last week' in Makkah.
facts.source_in_article: Saudi and Middle East media, as cited by Prothom Alo

facts.statement: Bangladesh asked the Saudi ambassador why it was not informed before the sentences were carried out; government sources consider that the rule of informing the country concerned before trying and punishing a foreign national was not followed in this case.
facts.source_in_article: Government sources / senior foreign ministry officials

facts.statement: Foreign ministry secretary (bilateral affairs) Md. Nazrul Islam met Saudi ambassador Abdullah bin Zafar H bin Abiyah at State Guest House Padma, Dhaka, from 3:30 pm for about half an hour, and a diplomatic note seeking information on the two executed Bangladeshis was handed to the ambassador.
facts.source_in_article: Md. Nazrul Islam (confirmed meeting); senior foreign ministry officials

facts.statement: The Saudi ambassador said he would get details from the Saudi foreign ministry in Riyadh and then inform Bangladesh.

The same diplomatic note was sent on Thursday (15 October 2026) from the Bangladesh Consul General's office in Jeddah to the Saudi foreign ministry there; on 18 October the office formally requested a discussion with the ministry's local official, and a meeting was expected within a day or two.
facts.source_in_article: Source at the Bangladesh Consul General's office in Jeddah

facts.statement: As of 18 October 2026 it was not clear whether the Saudi authorities had formally told Bangladesh anything about the charge; a related headline says Bangladesh did not know of the executions beforehand.

headline_en: What is the police's problem if an unmarried woman goes abroad?
summary_en: A column discusses a High Court rule issued on Tuesday (29 September 2026) asking why immigration police's stopping of three adult women from travelling to Nepal should not be declared without lawful authority. The women had valid passports, entry permission, tickets and hotel bookings but were questioned about being unmarried and travelling without a guardian. The writer argues such gender-based questioning at immigration is unconstitutional.

facts.statement: The High Court issued a rule asking why the immigration police's action in preventing three adult women from travelling abroad should not be declared to be without lawful authority, ordered disposal of the women's complaint, and asked why proper guidelines should not be framed so that adult women citizens' lawful foreign travel is not obstructed merely for being unmarried, travelling without a guardian or similar gender-based considerations.
facts.source_in_article: High Court rule, as described by columnist Monzurul Islam

facts.statement: The three adult women wanted to travel together to Nepal with valid passports, visa or entry permission, air tickets and hotel bookings and no court ban; immigration officers asked whether their families knew of the trip, told them to phone home, questioned their being unmarried and travelling without a guardian, and finally did not let them go.
After the incident the three women complained in writing to the Additional Inspector General of Police and got no response; a legal notice also went unanswered, after which they went to court.

Women's rights activist Ferdous Ara Rumee wrote on Facebook of an earlier case: five women with all documents were going to Nepal for a leadership workshop; an immigration officer asked one whether her husband knew, was not satisfied by her yes, took the husband's phone number, called him to confirm and only then let her go, though she headed an organisation.
facts.source_in_article: Ferdous Ara Rumee (Facebook), cited by the columnist

facts.statement: The columnist cites the Constitution: Article 27 (equality before law), Article 28 (no discrimination on grounds of sex), Articles 31 and 32 (protection of law and personal liberty) and Article 36 (freedom of movement and to leave the country), and says immigration police may check for trafficking, forged papers, fleeing offenders or legal bans but suspicion must rest on facts and law, not on whether a traveller is unmarried or alone.
The columnist notes that it is unknown how many women harassed in the same way at immigration turned back without protest and lost their ticket and hotel booking money.

headline_en: Silver economy: how ready is Bangladesh for a trillion-dollar market?
summary_en: A column by Mohammad Jalal Uddin Sikder (North South University) describes the 'silver economy' of ageing societies and the projected shortages of care workers in the EU, Germany, Japan, South Korea and the US, and how China, India and the Philippines are responding. It proposes that Bangladesh form a national task force, convert some TTCs into caregiving academies with language training, and also export products and services.

facts.statement: More than 20-22 lakh young people enter Bangladesh's labour market every year, according to the World Bank's 2019 'Skilling Up Bangladesh's Youth for a Changing Job Market' and the ILO's 2021 'A Boost to Skills Training in Bangladesh'.
facts.source_in_article: World Bank 2019 and ILO 2021, cited by columnist

facts.statement: Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare said in 2024 that Japan had about 21 lakh 50 thousand care workers in 2022, will need about 24 lakh in 2026 and 27 lakh 20 thousand in 2040, i.e. about 5 lakh 70 thousand more.
facts.source_in_article: Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (2024), cited by columnist

facts.statement: Germany may need about 21 lakh 50 thousand care workers in 2049; by Destatis's 2024 estimate a shortfall of 2 lakh 80 thousand to 6 lakh 90 thousand people may remain. Destatis also says a large part of the baby-boomer generation will leave the job market in the next 10 to 15 years.
facts.source_in_article: Destatis (German federal statistics office), cited by columnist

facts.statement: Korea Development Institute (KDI) researcher Junghyun Kwon's 2026 study 'Eldercare Workforce: Projections and Policy Implications' shows South Korea may need about 3 lakh 32 thousand more care workers in 2033 and about 9 lakh 90 thousand more in 2043 to keep the current workload; KDI recommends easing the route for bringing in foreign workers as well as using care robots.

The European Commission's 2021 'Green Paper on Ageing' says about one in five people in the EU is over 65, possibly about one in three around 2070; the Commission's 'European Care Strategy' says more than 16 lakh additional workers must be added by 2050 just to maintain current long-term care.

US Bureau of Labor Statistics projections speak of several lakh job openings every year in home health and personal care aide occupations; not all are new posts, the figure combines retirements, job leavers and new jobs.

The World Economic Forum (26 August 2026, citing World Data Lab) says the world market for products and services made specially for older people is about USD 4.5 trillion, growing about 7% a year; people over 60 are 15% of world population but will account for about 27% of consumer spending, USD 19 trillion, in 2026.
facts.source_in_article: World Economic Forum / World Data Lab, cited by columnist

facts.statement: The Philippines has long used its Economic Partnership Agreement with Japan to train and send nurses and caregivers, including Japanese language teaching and preparing workers for the destination country's professional examinations.

India's Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment runs a 'Training of Geriatric Caregivers' programme to reduce the shortage of professionally trained workers; China's State Council issued a national policy paper on developing the silver economy in January 2024.

Bangladesh already has technical training centres (TTCs) under BMET, nursing education and private training institutions, and elderly caregiving training is being given under the National Skills Development Authority (NSDA); the columnist says these are scattered and not under one plan.

The columnist recommends a national task force (expatriates' welfare, health, education, commerce, industries and tourism ministries, BMET, NSDA, universities, business), converting some existing TTCs into specialised caregiving academies teaching Japanese, German, Korean and other needed languages and destination-country work rules, and partnering with foreign institutions and employers so that Bangladeshi certificates are accepted abroad.

The columnist notes a shortage of good trainers and language teachers in Bangladesh and suggests engaging skilled Bangladeshis abroad online for paid classes, and expanding honours, master's, diploma and short courses in geriatric care, elder care management and rehabilitation.

headline_en: One arrested on charge of taking a man to Saudi Arabia with promise of a good job and torturing him
summary_en: CID's human trafficking unit arrested Md. Salman Hossain (33) at Dhaka airport on Monday 31 August 2026. According to the case, a ring took BDT 6 lakh from a man promising a good job at a fast-food shop in Saudi Arabia, sent him on 7 June of the previous year, gave him no job, confined and beat him in a house while demanding more money for an iqama; he escaped, was later detained by Saudi police and was sent back on 22 July.

facts.statement: A ring took BDT 6 lakh from a man by promising him a good job at a fast-food shop in Saudi Arabia and sent him there on 7 June of 'last year' (2025); after arrival he was not given the promised job.

According to CID, Salman Hossain and other ring members confined the victim in a house in Saudi Arabia, then demanded more money from his family saying it was to arrange his iqama (legal residence permit), and physically tortured him to extract the money.
The victim escaped from the house by a ruse, took shelter with a local person in a desert area, was later detained by Saudi police and was sent back to Bangladesh on 22 July (2026).
CID's human trafficking unit arrested Md. Salman Hossain (33), described as a member of a human-trafficking ring, at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, at midday on Monday 31 August 2026.
facts.source_in_article: CID Special Superintendent (Media) Md. Sufi Ullah (ছুফি উল্লাহ), press release

facts.statement: The victim's wife filed a case under the human trafficking law at Savar police station; CID says its preliminary investigation found Salman directly involved and that the victim was held in Salman's own house in Saudi Arabia. Investigation continues to identify other accused, absconders and local and foreign associates.

headline_en: Family thought he was dead; Farid, who went abroad as a child, returns after 25 years
summary_en: Mohammad Farid of Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar, crossed illegally to Pakistan via India with his father at age 10, lost both legs in a train accident there, was taken to Turkey by traffickers promising Europe, and lived there irregularly selling water until Turkish police deported him. He landed in Dhaka on 18 August 2026 unable to identify himself; the airport's Probashi Kallyan Desk passed him to BRAC's Ashkona Migration Welfare Centre, which traced his family within 12 hours.

facts.statement: Mohammad Farid, then aged 10, crossed the border illegally with his father and went via India to Pakistan, where the two looked for a livelihood; in Pakistan he was run over by a train and doctors had to amputate both his legs.

A human-trafficking ring lured Farid, after he lost his legs in Pakistan, with talk of a better life and a job and of taking him to Europe, and at one point took him to Turkey, where he sold water on the seashore and lived as an irregular migrant.

Turkish law-enforcement recently detained Farid and sent him back to Bangladesh; he arrived at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport, Dhaka, on a flight from Turkey at about 5:15 am on 18 August (2026). The article also says he returned 'last Thursday', which does not match 18 August.
facts.source_in_article: BRAC Migration Programme sources; Prothom Alo report

facts.statement: Having lived abroad since childhood, Farid could give only his own and his parents' names and the address 'Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar'. Members of the Civil Aviation Authority's Aviation Security (AVSEC) force handed him through the airport's Probashi Kallyan Desk to BRAC's Ashkona Migration Welfare Centre.

BRAC Migration Programme staff, with help from local public representatives and journalists, traced Farid's family at Maricchya Palong Nasir Para, Ukhiya, Cox's Bazar, within 12 hours; identity was confirmed over a video call by a sixth finger on one hand, and he was handed to his younger brother Syed Alam in Dhaka and taken to his mother Nurjahan Begum in Cox's Bazar. His father Ayub Ali is still in Pakistan.

BRAC associate director (Migration and Youth Platform) Shariful Islam Hasan said that in the past eight years BRAC has assisted 41 thousand migrants at the airport, and has safely handed 164 migrants like Farid over to their families.

A T M Mahbubul Karim, project director of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board's RAISE project and a joint secretary, said Mohammad Farid would be given necessary assistance; BRAC said it wants to do more for him in the long term so he can get back on his feet.
facts.source_in_article: A T M Mahbubul Karim; Shariful Islam Hasan

facts.statement: Services named in the article for returnees in distress at Dhaka airport: the Probashi Kallyan Desk at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport (deputy director Shariful Islam) and BRAC's Migration Welfare Centre at Ashkona.

headline_en: 'Probashi Card' to launch on trial next month; the benefits it will carry
summary_en: A meeting chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Saturday 18 July 2026 decided to launch the 'Probashi Card' on a pilot basis in August, starting with a Probashi debit card issued through Janata Bank. The deputy press secretary listed airport, travel, health, repatriation-of-body, insurance, remittance and priority-service benefits and targets of 50,000 cards by December and two lakh by June of the next year.

facts.statement: A meeting on the Probashi Card chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman decided that the government will start the 'Probashi Card' project on a pilot basis within August 2026; the pilot launch is to be in the middle of that month.
facts.source_in_article: Shahadat Hossain Swadhin, deputy press secretary to the Prime Minister

facts.statement: In the first phase a Probashi debit card will be issued through Janata Bank; in the second phase all Probashi Card activities will be done through Probashi Kallyan Bank.
Targets set for the Probashi Card: 50 thousand cards distributed by December (2026) and two lakh by June of the next year.
facts.source_in_article: Deputy press secretary Shahadat Hossain, reporting the meeting

facts.statement: The stated purpose of the Probashi Card is social dignity, empowerment and financial incentives for expatriates, and international payment and banking facilities through a 'dual currency card'.

Airport and travel benefits listed for the Probashi Card: complimentary airport lounge use at home and abroad, fast service through special immigration booths, complimentary 'meet and greet' at international airports, discounts on air tickets and hotel bookings, fair-priced car booking at home and abroad, and 'airport pick and drop' on the Signature card.
Listed Probashi Card benefits include free transport of the body on the cardholder's death, rehabilitation opportunities for returnees and insurance cover.

Other listed Probashi Card benefits: expatriate service booths at government hospitals and discounts at private ones; priority in land registration, mutation, utilities, licences and foreign investment; remittance reward points, credit scoring and loan facilities; sending money directly through the card and easy transactions; priority in NID, passport and consular services; and other bank and government benefits.

At the meeting the Prime Minister directed that the National Skills Development Authority be made up to date and modern and that Bangladeshi expatriates across the world be brought under the Probashi Card. The card is described as an election pledge, alongside the Family, Farmer and Sports cards already begun (per state news agency BSS).
facts.source_in_article: Deputy press secretary Shahadat Hossain; BSS

headline_en: Bodies of 5 Bangladeshis killed in road accident in Qatar brought home
summary_en: The bodies of five Bangladeshis from Kanaighat, Sylhet, killed in a road accident in the Shahaniya area of Qatar on the morning of 21 June 2026, arrived at Sylhet's Osmani International Airport on Tuesday 30 June on Biman flight BG-226. The Wage Earners' Welfare Board financed the repatriation.

facts.statement: Five Bangladeshi expatriates were killed in a road accident in the Shahaniya area of Qatar on the morning of 21 June 2026: Abdul Kadir of Gachhbari village, Mustaq Ahmed Afnan and Zubair Ahmed of Majhtaluk village, Jasim Uddin of Agataluk village and Jibal Ahmed of Amarpur village, all in Kanaighat upazila, Sylhet.
facts.source_in_article: Labour welfare wing, Bangladesh embassy in Qatar; BSS

facts.statement: The five bodies were sent home with financing from the Bangladesh Wage Earners' Welfare Board; a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight (BG-226) left Hamad International Airport, Qatar, on the night of Monday 29 June 2026 and reached M A G Osmani International Airport, Sylhet, on the morning of 30 June.
The ministry's relevant branch was said to be working on handing the bodies over to the families properly and providing 'other benefits'.

headline_en: Expatriate Bangladeshi Mehedi Hasan receives 'Partner of the Labour Movement Award' in Singapore
summary_en: Md. Mehedi Hasan of Nandail, Mymensingh, received the NTUC 'Partner of the Labour Movement' May Day Award in Singapore on Wednesday (about 13 May 2026) for his volunteer work with the NTUC Migrant Workers' Centre (MWC). The article describes his outreach to migrant workers on scams, workplace safety and accident assistance.

facts.statement: Expatriate Bangladeshi Md. Mehedi Hasan, of Achargaon village, Nandail upazila, Mymensingh, received the NTUC 'Partner of the Labour Movement' May Day Award from NTUC Secretary-General Ng Chee Meng at the Orchid Country Club Grand Ballroom, Singapore.

The NTUC Migrant Workers' Centre (MWC) in Singapore has a membership for migrant workers and welfare activities; Mehedi Hasan promotes MWC membership and volunteers with FairPrice, the People's Association, the Singapore Police Force, dormitory operators and charities, and conveys messages to migrant workers on scam awareness, workplace safety and the channels for assistance after accidents, and on Singapore's rules.
The first Bangladeshi to receive NTUC's Partner of the Labour Movement Award in Singapore was Sumon Biswas of Mahajanpur village, Mujibnagar thana, Meherpur, in 2025.

headline_en: Remittances above USD 3 billion for five straight months
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data released on Sunday 3 May 2026 show remittances of USD 312.70 crore in April, the fifth consecutive month above USD 3 billion, after a record USD 375 crore in March. The article attributes higher inflows to Eid and the Middle East war (Iran versus the US and Israel), which also raised the dollar's exchange rate, and reports economists' advice to hold reserves.

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh in April 2026 were USD 312 crore 70 lakh (over USD 3 billion), making five consecutive months above USD 3 billion since December.

Monthly remittances to Bangladesh: December USD 322 crore, January USD 317 crore, February USD 302 crore, March USD 375 crore. March's USD 3.75 billion is the highest ever and 14% more than March of the previous year.

The article says expatriates sent more money than before because of Eid-ul-Fitr and the war in the Middle East between Iran and the United States and Israel; bankers expect the trend to continue in May for Eid-ul-Azha.
Because of the Middle East crisis the dollar's exchange rate against the taka has risen, so remitters are getting a higher price for US dollars sent as remittance.
Eight noted economists advised the Bangladesh Bank governor to hold on to foreign exchange reserves to absorb a possible shock from the war and not to cut the policy interest rate yet.
facts.source_in_article: Economists at a meeting with the Bangladesh Bank governor

headline_en: Special drive to be run to eradicate human trafficking and drugs: home minister in Teknaf
summary_en: Speaking at a farmer-card distribution event in Teknaf on Tuesday 14 April 2026, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said human trafficking by illegal routes has increased and that special drives against trafficking and drugs will soon be run on the Teknaf-Ukhiya coast of Cox's Bazar and other risky areas. He said points used for the crime will be identified and law enforcers have been instructed.

facts.statement: Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said human trafficking by illegal routes has increased and that a special drive to eradicate human trafficking and drugs will soon be run in risky areas of the country including the Teknaf-Ukhiya coast of Cox's Bazar.
facts.source_in_article: Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed, at Teknaf

facts.statement: The home minister said some areas of Teknaf, Ukhiya and Cox's Bazar have been identified as risky for human trafficking; law enforcers have been given instructions, the points used for these crimes will be identified and organised, planned operations run, with regular drives to bring offenders to justice.

headline_en: Government working to reactivate labour markets in Malaysia and other countries: expatriates' welfare minister
summary_en: In Sylhet on Sunday 12 April 2026, Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the government has moved to reopen the long-closed Malaysian labour market quickly and is negotiating visa extensions for workers who have returned. He also ordered quick action to stop harassment of passengers at Sylhet Osmani International Airport.

facts.statement: Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said the government is working to reactivate labour markets in Malaysia and other countries, and that an initiative has been taken to reopen Malaysia's long-closed labour market quickly.
facts.source_in_article: Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury, to reporters in Sylhet

facts.statement: On his Malaysia visit and talks, the minister said 'we have signed a joint venture, it is in our favour' and that the meeting held was very fruitful.

The minister said the government is discussing visa extensions for workers who have come back, and that where there are visa problems it is working diplomatically with various countries to extend visa validity.

At the Sylhet law-and-order committee meeting the minister specially instructed the authorities to take effective steps very quickly to stop harassment of passengers at Sylhet Osmani International Airport.
